Mount Etna. Located on the east coast of Sicily, Italy, Mount Etna is the highest active volcano in Europe outside the Caucasus Mountains, dominating the skyline of eastern Sicily near the city of Catania. One of the most active volcanoes in the world, it is in a state of near-constant activity and has a recorded history of eruptions dating back to fifteen hundred BC. In ancient Greek mythology, Etna was believed to be the prison of the monster Typhon, who was defeated and buried under the mountain by Zeus, with Etna's eruptions representing his fiery struggles. The volcano was also the mythological home of the forge of Hephaestus, also known as Vulcan, where the Cyclopes crafted thunderbolts for Zeus. Mount Etna is linked to the death of the philosopher Empedocles, who according to legend threw himself into the volcano's crater in 430 BC to prove his divinity, only for the volcano to spit back one of his bronze sandals. The volcano enjoys a long history of study, with its 1669 eruption being one of the first in history where humans successfully attempted to divert lava flows by digging trenches. Mount Etna is sister to Vesuvius, another active stratovolcano located on the Italian mainland in Campania, and shares volcanic features with the giants Zeus and Typhon from Greek myth.
